name: Fenugreek

card.summary: A culinary seed sold as an herbal testosterone and libido supplement; small trials of branded extracts report modest hormone changes, but evidence is limited.
card.note: Not considered safe in pregnancy; may lower blood sugar and interact with anticoagulant and diabetes drugs.

quick.overview:
Fenugreek is a Mediterranean and South Asian plant whose seeds are used as a spice and in traditional medicine. In looksmaxxing and fitness circles it is sold as a natural testosterone booster, usually as seed extract capsules.

A few small randomized trials of specific extracts, and meta-analyses of them, report increases in total testosterone or sexual-function scores in some men. Reviewers describe the evidence as limited by few studies, varied extracts and small samples.
quick.mechanism: Proponents attribute effects to steroidal saponins (such as protodioscin) and other seed compounds. Proposed mechanisms in the research literature include effects on androgen and estrogen pathways, though human mechanistic data are limited.
quick.risks: Reported side effects include diarrhea, bloating and gas, and a maple-like body odor. Wikipedia notes it may lower blood sugar and interfere with anticoagulants, and that it is not considered safe in pregnancy. It is sold as a dietary supplement in the US, not an approved drug.

lead: Fenugreek (Trigonella foenum-graecum) is an annual legume native to the Near East whose seeds and leaves are a staple spice and herb in South Asian, Middle Eastern and North African cooking [1]. It has a long record in traditional medicine, and the US National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health (NCCIH) puts its use as a spice and traditional remedy at about 6,000 years [2][15].

In appearance-focused and fitness communities, fenugreek seed extract is taken as an herbal testosterone and libido supplement, in the hope of supporting training, muscle, energy and a more masculine physique. It is also a common ingredient in multi-herb men's-health products alongside ashwagandha, tribulus and tongkat ali [4][5][11].

Several small randomized trials of specific extracts, and meta-analyses pooling them, report higher total testosterone or better sexual-function scores in some men; systematic reviews describe these findings as limited by few trials, differing extracts and small samples [3][14][16]. Wikipedia states that high-quality evidence for therapeutic properties is lacking and that the US FDA has not approved fenugreek for clinical use [1]. The NCCIH describes it as traditionally used for diabetes, menstrual cramps and milk supply and does not discuss testosterone [15].

paras: Seeds are roasted or ground into pickles, dals and spice blends such as panch phoron and sambar powder, and fresh leaves are eaten as a vegetable, for example in aloo methi; roasting softens the seeds' bitterness [1]. Other traditions use it too: seed powder coats cured beef (basturma) in Armenian and Turkish cooking, Iranian cooks use the leaves in ghormeh sabzi, Egyptians boil the seeds into a drink, Eritrean and Ethiopian cooks use it, and Yemenite Jews make a frothy seed relish (hilbah) eaten at Rosh Hashana [1].

Its maple-like aroma comes from sotolon, which is why the seeds appear in imitation maple flavouring [1]. Traditional medicine has used it as a digestive aid, for milk production and for menstrual cramps; Ethiopians also use the seeds medicinally for diabetes [1][2].

subs.h: Use in appearance and fitness communities
paras: Standardized seed extracts are sold alone or in blends with ashwagandha, tribulus, tongkat ali and other herbs for testosterone, libido and training support [2][5]. A US homeopathic-labelled oral spray on DailyMed lists fenugreek, at a 3X dilution, among a mix of herbs, animal-derived ingredients and testosterone at a 30X dilution; its label says it 'temporarily supports' testosterone output, that it has not been evaluated by the FDA, and that the FDA is not aware of scientific evidence supporting homeopathy [5].

The appearance logic proponents describe has three links: a rise in testosterone or libido, more drive and better recovery in training, and so more muscle and a leaner, more masculine look [4][11]. Fenugreek is also sometimes discussed for general digestive and blood-sugar reasons rather than for looks [11].

Cultivation probably began in the Near East, though the wild ancestor is unknown [1]. Charred seeds from Tell Halal in Iraq date to about 4000 BC, and seeds have also been found at Bronze Age Lachish and in Tutankhamun's tomb [1]. Cato the Elder listed it as fodder, a first-century Roman recipe flavours wine with it, Josephus described it as a staple in first-century Galilee, and the second-century Mishnah mentions it under the Hebrew name tiltan [1]. Grokipedia, an AI-generated encyclopedia, places its earliest medical documentation in the Ebers Papyrus [2].

India is now the largest producer, with more than 80 percent of its output from Rajasthan [1]. In 2011 sprouts grown from fenugreek seed imported from Egypt were linked to an E. coli O104:H4 outbreak in Germany and France [1].

Seeds contain steroidal saponins including diosgenin, a precursor used in pharmaceutical steroid synthesis, along with fiber, galactomannan and the alkaloid trigonelline [2][9][10]. Proposed mechanisms for testosterone-related effects, such as effects on enzymes that convert androgens to estrogens, come mainly from laboratory work; research on trigonelline and diosgenin has focused on diabetes and cancer models [9][10].

A 2020 meta-analysis of four clinical trials in men reported that fenugreek extract had a significant effect on total serum testosterone [14]. A 2016 double-blind placebo-controlled trial of 120 men aged 43 to 70 found that a 12-week course of the branded extract Testofen was associated with lower androgen-deficiency symptom scores, better sexual-function scores and higher total and free testosterone than placebo [3].

A 2024 double-blind trial of the extract Trigozim randomised 95 men aged 40 to 80 to placebo or one of three amounts for 12 weeks. Plasma total testosterone and free testosterone index rose from baseline at every level, but plasma differences against placebo were not statistically significant; saliva testosterone was about 37 percent higher than placebo across levels, 19.6 percent higher at the top level, and the top level raised the free testosterone index about 12 percent [16]. The investigators reported no side effects; the study was funded by a company whose employees and shareholders include several authors, and the company ran the intervention and most lab analyses [16].

A 2021 systematic review of 32 studies on 13 herbs found that fenugreek seed extract and ashwagandha root extract showed positive effects on testosterone in men, but concluded that the evidence is limited by few studies per herb, varied extracts and doses, and small samples [3]. A 2023 systematic review of six randomized trials on muscle performance found that four reported gains in strength, endurance or lean mass with fenugreek glycoside or saponin preparations, while two small trials of fewer than ten participants examined glycogen resynthesis; its authors noted doping rules and possible liver and kidney effects [3].

ClinicalTrials.gov lists a completed trial of fenugreek supplementation in men with testosterone deficiency (n=58) and trials in diabetes, lactation, polycystic ovary syndrome and obesity [6]. Wikipedia describes studies of blood-sugar effects as of limited quality and says as of 2023 no strong evidence supports use for menstrual pain or milk supply; the NCCIH reports mixed results for breast milk and many low-quality diabetes studies [1][15].
Reported side effects include diarrhea, bloating, gas and sweating, and a maple-like odor of sweat, urine or breast milk. People allergic to peanuts or chickpeas may react [1].

Fenugreek may lower blood sugar and so interact with antidiabetic drugs, and the NCCIH notes that large amounts may cause a harmful drop in blood sugar and that allergic reactions, sometimes serious, occur [1][15]. Its coumarin-like compounds may affect anticoagulant and antiplatelet drugs; reviews of herb-drug interactions have discussed warfarin and analgesic interactions [1][7][8]. Wikipedia and the NCCIH state that it is not safe in amounts above food levels during pregnancy, citing possible uterine effects and a link to birth defects, and it may be unsafe for women with hormone-sensitive cancers [1][15].
Fenugreek is sold in the US as a food and dietary supplement; supplements are not approved by the FDA before sale, so quality and labeling can vary [1][15].

Forum users on looksmax.org have asked whether it is worth taking for testosterone or libido, with replies ranging from personal reports of improved lifts to suspicion that it is a 'cope' [4][11][12]. It appears in short threads together with ashwagandha, reflecting how herbal testosterone products are usually bundled [4]. The 2021 systematic review that identified fenugreek seed extract and ashwagandha root extract as the two herbs with positive testosterone findings is the research most often relevant to these discussions [3].

Fenugreek is discussed with other herbal testosterone-support supplements, including ashwagandha, tribulus and tongkat ali, and with prescription routes such as testosterone replacement therapy, which is a separate medical treatment [4][5].

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, fenugreek appears in short threads asking whether herbal testosterone boosters work, often alongside ashwagandha [4][11].

claims.believers: Some users report that their lifts increased after taking it and that it "increases test" [11].
claims.experts: A 2020 meta-analysis of four trials found a significant effect of extract on total testosterone, but a 2021 systematic review called the evidence limited by small samples and varied extracts [3].

claims.claim: A herbal pill for more testosterone sounds like a cope
claims.believers: Skeptical forum users say that a herbal pill for testosterone sounds like a "cope" and may give a placebo effect on libido, while another thread's original poster asks whether it is worth buying if the effect is placebo [4][12].
claims.experts: Placebo-controlled trials exist for specific extracts; their authors reported benefit over placebo, while reviewers note limited and heterogeneous evidence [3].

claims.claim: Fenugreek is useful for specific problems such as erectile or digestive issues rather than for general testosterone
claims.believers: One commenter suggested it is unneeded unless a person has erectile, kidney or digestive problems [11].
claims.experts: Published research has examined it mainly in diabetes, lactation and androgen-related symptoms, with limited-quality evidence [1][3].

claims.claim: Fenugreek improves libido and sexual function
claims.believers: Users and supplement marketers list libido as a main benefit, and some forum posters say it improved sexual performance [4][11].
claims.experts: The 2016 Testofen trial reported better sexual-function scores than placebo in men aged 43 to 70 [3]; the NCCIH lists no sexual indication [15].

claims.claim: Fenugreek is a safe natural alternative to testosterone therapy
claims.believers: Proponents frame herbs as a gentler option than prescription hormones [5].
claims.experts: Fenugreek is not an approved drug for testosterone deficiency, and sources list blood-sugar lowering, drug interactions and pregnancy cautions [1][15].

angle.text: People take fenugreek extract hoping to raise testosterone, which they link to training progress, muscle and libido. Trials of standardised extracts have measured testosterone and sexual-function scores in men; results vary by product [3][16].
